issues.legal_issue: A surplus from the sale of depreciable business assets after business cessation is taxable under the second proviso only if the business was carried on and the assets were used for it during at least part of the relevant previous year.
material_facts: The company’s business was completely closed in December 1954.
The liquidator sold the company’s buildings, plant and machinery in March 1955 for more than their written-down values.
The relevant accounting year was calendar year 1955, during which the company carried on no business.
The tax authority sought to tax the surplus as deemed profits under the second proviso to section 10(2)(vii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.
issues.conclusion: The proviso did not apply to the surplus because the company carried on no business during any part of the accounting year. The amendment permitting a sale after cessation of business removed only the requirement that the sale occur while the business continued; it did not remove the requirements that the business be carried on and the assets be used for it during at least part of the previous year.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 10(1) and 10(2)(vii), including its second proviso as amended by Act 67 of 1949, the surplus is deemed to be profits of the previous year only where the business was carried on and the relevant building, machinery or plant was used for that business during at least part of that year. The amendment removed the requirement that the sale precede cessation of business, not the business-activity and asset-use requirements. “Previous year” retains its meaning under section 2(11)(b) in this context. The proviso’s deeming fiction is limited to its purpose and cannot be extended to deem a business or asset use that did not occur. The Court relied on The Liquidators of Pursa Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Commissioner of Income-tax v. Express Newspapers Ltd., Cape Brandy Syndicate v. I.R.C., Commissioner of Income-tax v. Indo-Mercantile Bank Ltd., Additional Income-tax Officer v. E. Alfred, Commissioner of Income-tax v. Amarchand N. Shroff, Dandhania Kedia & Co. v. C.I.T., and Commissioner of Income-tax v. K. Srinivasan and K. Gopalan.

predicates.asset_sale_surplus_tax_assessment: A tax assessment seeks to treat a surplus from the sale of depreciable business assets as business profits.
predicates.business_carried_on_during_accounting_ye: The assessee carried on the relevant business during at least part of the accounting year.
predicates.asset_used_for_business_during_accountin: The assets that produced the sale surplus were used for the relevant business during at least part of the accounting year.

issues.definition: When an assessment seeks to tax a depreciable-asset sale surplus as business profits, the surplus is not taxable under the proviso if the business was not carried on or the assets were not used for it during the accounting year.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may set aside a tax tribunal’s factual estimate in a statutory reference when the estimate has no evidentiary material to support it.
material_facts: The tax tribunal rejected the expert valuation of the buildings and estimated a higher sale value.
The tribunal’s estimate rested on assumptions and surmise, with no material supporting its grounds or the value it selected.
The valuation question was referred to the High Court under the income-tax reference procedure.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was entitled to go behind the tribunal’s unsupported finding and answer the referred question; the tribunal’s estimate of the buildings’ sale value could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: In a reference under section 66 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, the High Court may interfere with a tribunal’s factual finding when it is not based on evidence or other material, and may answer the referred question accordingly. No earlier case was cited for this ruling.

predicates.income_tax_reference: A question arising from a tax tribunal’s decision is before the High Court in a statutory reference.
predicates.tribunal_factual_finding_lacks_evidentia: The tribunal’s factual finding is based on surmise or assumption rather than supporting evidence or other material.

issues.definition: In a statutory tax reference, the High Court may set aside a tribunal’s factual finding when the finding lacks evidentiary support.
